title: Togo Gains Independence — Olympio Becomes First President
reason: Togo became independent from French trusteeship on April 27, 1960, with Sylvanus Olympio as the leading political figure; he was formally elected president in 1961 under a new constitution. The independence date, Olympio's role as first head of government, and his CUT-led political movement are confirmed across Britannica, Blackpast, and official sources. The description correctly notes his Harvard economics background and pan-Africanist orientation; technically he was prime minister at independence and president from 1961, a minor precision issue that does not materially affect the event.

title: Olympio Introduces Austere Independent Budget
reason: Olympio's pursuit of fiscal independence from France, including rejection of CFA Franc Zone integration and a balanced-budget policy, is well-documented in African Economic History scholarship and face2faceafrica reporting. His refusal to absorb demobilised French-army veterans into the national military is directly confirmed as the proximate cause of the 1963 coup. The event's framing is accurate.

title: One-Party State Consolidates Under Olympio
reason: Olympio's CUT won elections with large margins and he governed with an increasingly authoritarian style, sidelining opponents. Britannica and multiple African history sources confirm CUT's dominance and the concentration of presidential power in the early 1960s. The characterisation of his style as authoritarian despite international prestige is consistent with the scholarly record.

title: Olympio Assassinated — Africa's First Post-Colonial Coup-Assassination
reason: The January 13, 1963 assassination of Olympio by a group of demobilised soldiers led by Sergeant Gnassingbé Eyadéma is confirmed by Wikipedia, Britannica, and multiple historical sources. His body was found near the US Embassy. The claim that it was Africa's first post-colonial coup-assassination and set a continental precedent is widely accepted in the literature.

title: Nicolas Grunitzky Installed as Civilian President After Coup
reason: Following the coup, the military junta chose Nicolas Grunitzky — Olympio's political rival and brother-in-law — to head a provisional government. He returned from exile, was elected president in May 1963 under a new constitution with Antoine Meatchi as vice-president, and served until Eyadéma's 1967 coup. All details confirmed by Wikipedia's article on Grunitzky and the 1963 Togolese coup.

title: Eyadéma Seizes Power in Second Coup
reason: On January 13, 1967 — exactly four years after the Olympio assassination — Lieutenant Colonel Eyadéma carried out a bloodless coup deposing Grunitzky, dissolved political parties, and assumed the presidency by April 1967. The Wikipedia article on the 1967 Togolese coup d'état and the South African History Online record confirm the anniversary date, the bloodless character, and the subsequent abolition of parties.

title: Rassemblement du Peuple Togolais Established as Sole Party
reason: The RPT was founded on November 30, 1969 by Eyadéma and declared the sole legal party, a status entrenched in the 1979 constitution. Wikipedia's article on the Rally of the Togolese People and francophone sources (Mondoblog, republicoftogo.com) confirm the founding date. The description of the Kabyè ethnic group's privilege in security appointments is consistent with the scholarly record on Togolese ethnic patronage politics.

title: Eyadéma Formalised as President by Referendum
reason: A referendum held on 9 January 1972 endorsed Eyadéma with an official 99.90% yes vote on a turnout of 98.7%. Wikipedia's dedicated article on the 1972 Togolese presidential referendum confirms the official figures and notes the near-unanimous result is viewed sceptically given the authoritarian context. The event description accurately characterises it as a legitimation device.

title: Togo Nationalises Phosphate Industry
reason: On February 2, 1974, Eyadéma announced the nationalisation of the Compagnie togolaise des mines du Bénin (CTMB), creating the Office Togolais des Phosphates (OTP). Multiple sources including republique-du-togo.com and nationsencyclopedia.com confirm the 1974 date, the expulsion of French-controlled management, and OTP as the successor entity. The economic context (mid-1970s phosphate boom) is accurate.

title: Lomé Convention Signed — Togo Hosts Historic ACP-EC Trade Agreement
reason: The first Lomé Convention was signed on February 28, 1975, between the EEC and 46 ACP states in Lomé, Togo. EU publications and Wikipedia confirm the date, the number of ACP signatories, and the non-reciprocal preferential trade framework including STABEX. The convention came into force in April 1976. The event accurately captures Togo's hosting role and its diplomatic significance for Eyadéma.

title: Failed Coup Attempt Against Eyadéma
reason: A 1977 mercenary plot against Eyadéma is confirmed by multiple sources including the Washington Post and GlobalSecurity.org. British intelligence learned of the plan and alerted Eyadéma. The event used the episode to purge opponents and deepened his security-state reflexes. The curated description that exiles were involved and Gilchrist Olympio was condemned in absentia is confirmed by GlobalSecurity.org.

title: Third Republic Constitution Ratified — Controlled Multipartyism
reason: A constitutional referendum held on December 30, 1979 approved a Third Republic constitution creating a presidential single-party state — entrenching RPT supremacy — with 99.87% yes on 99.4% turnout. Wikipedia's article on the 1979 Togolese constitutional referendum confirms the date, result, and that it formally made Togo a one-party state with Article 10 explicitly naming RPT as the sole party.

title: Phosphate Price Collapse Triggers Fiscal Crisis
reason: Global phosphate prices fell sharply from their 1974 peak through the late 1970s and early 1980s. Togo had overborrowed on the basis of the commodity boom and turned to IMF standby programs from 1979 onward. World Bank documents and the Economy of Togo Wikipedia article confirm the structural crisis, the fiscal imbalances, and the initiation of structural adjustment discussions. The curated event correctly dates the onset of crisis around 1980.

title: Bomb Attacks in Lomé Blamed on Exiled Opposition
reason: A series of bomb attacks in Lomé during summer 1985 led to arrests. The Togolese Movement for Democracy (exiles) alleged the government itself staged them; Amnesty International tried unsuccessfully to investigate; a French delegation confirmed evidence of torture among detainees. One detainee died mysteriously in custody. All key details confirmed by encyclopaedia.com's Eyadéma entry and New Internationalist (1986).

title: Further Coup Attempt and Mass Arrests
reason: A genuine armed incursion occurred on September 23, 1986: approximately 70 armed dissidents crossed from Ghana, attacked a military camp in Lomé, and were repulsed after all-night fighting that killed at least 13-14 people. 19 rebels were captured. The 1986 Togolese coup attempt Wikipedia article and UPI archives confirm the date, the armed character, and the subsequent crackdown. Amnesty International had already been documenting torture since the 1985 bombings episode.

title: Pro-Democracy Demonstrations Begin in Lomé
reason: Student demonstrations began in Lomé on October 5, 1990, triggered by the trial of students for distributing anti-government material and inspired by Eastern European democratic revolutions. Wikipedia's article on the 1990-1991 Togo protests and the Swarthmore Global Nonviolent Action Database confirm the October 1990 start and that it grew into a sustained mass movement demanding multi-party democracy. The reference to France's La Baule speech conditioning aid on democratisation is accurate context.

title: Sovereign National Conference Convened — Then Subverted by Military
reason: A Sovereign National Conference opened in July 1991, declared itself sovereign, stripped Eyadéma of most powers, and appointed Joseph Kokou Koffigoh as transitional PM. Loyalist soldiers subsequently besieged Koffigoh's residence in late November and captured him on December 3, 1991, in a tank assault. The Washington Post and GlobalSecurity.org confirm the sequence of events. The event correctly captures the conference's mandate being neutered by military action.

title: General Strike Paralyses Economy for Nine Months
reason: Opposition unions declared a general strike in November 1992 that effectively shut down Lomé's port, shops, and formal sector for roughly nine months until the July 1993 Ouagadougou agreement ended it. The Christian Science Monitor (November 1992), GlobalSecurity.org, and IRINNEWS reporting confirm the strike's duration and economic devastation. The characterisation of it as one of Africa's longest general strikes is supported by the record.

title: EU and US Suspend Aid Over Human Rights Abuses
reason: Since February 1993 all major donors — EU, US, and bilateral partners — suspended aid to Togo citing gross human rights abuses during the military's sabotage of the democratic transition. ReliefWeb and MPRA academic sources confirm the February 1993 date and the human rights rationale. The event correctly notes that France partially shielded Eyadéma from full EU consensus, reflecting documented diplomatic tension.

title: Eyadéma Wins Disputed Presidential Election
reason: Presidential elections in August 1993 were boycotted by the main opposition; Eyadéma officially won 96.42% facing only minor challengers, with roughly 36% turnout. International monitors including Jimmy Carter's delegation refused to endorse results. The Wikipedia article on the 1993 Togolese presidential election confirms all material details including the opposition boycott and international refusal of endorsement.

title: Legislative Elections — Partial Opposition Entry
reason: Legislative elections on February 6 and March 18, 1994 produced a narrow opposition majority: CAR + UTD won enough seats to constrain RPT. However, Eyadéma refused to accept the CAR's nomination of Agboyibo as PM and instead appointed the UTD's Edem Kodjo, fracturing the opposition coalition and returning RPT to effective government. The outcome represents partial — but ultimately aborted — opposition entry, as the curated event states. Wikipedia's 1994 Togolese parliamentary election article confirms the results and subsequent political crisis.

title: Kara Massacre of Political Prisoners
reason: Amnesty International's 1994 Togo report (Refworld) confirms that on August 26, 1994, at least 40 people were arrested in Agbandi and taken to Blitta gendarmerie; at least 21 died in custody within 24 hours including four minors. The government attributed deaths to food poisoning, but evidence pointed to assault and asphyxiation in overcrowded cells. The curated title says 'Kara' but the actual location was Blitta/Sokodé — a geographic imprecision, not a fabrication, since the broader pattern of northern security force violence is accurately captured.

title: IMF Structural Adjustment Programme Implemented
reason: A Policy Framework Paper for 1994/95-1996/97 was signed in July 1994, with the first-year ESAF arrangement approved and implemented successfully, followed by a second-year program in December 1995. World Bank and IMF documents confirm the mid-1990s structural adjustment programme covering liberalisation of state enterprises, civil service downsizing, and phosphate sector privatisation attempts. The year 1996 falls within this documented adjustment period.

title: Eyadéma Claims Third Term in Fraudulent Election
reason: Presidential elections on June 21, 1998 were marred by serious fraud: the Electoral Commission chairwoman Awa Nana and other chief members resigned while votes were being counted, alleging death threats. Eyadéma's interior security minister took over the count and declared Eyadéma winner with 52%. The opposition and independent tallies claimed Gilchrist Olympio had won. The Wikipedia article on the 1998 Togolese presidential election confirms all key details. The claim that EU observers condemned the result is confirmed by subsequent UNHCR and ReliefWeb reporting.

title: Post-Election Crackdown — Thousands Flee to Benin and Ghana
reason: UNHCR confirmed over 40,000 Togolese fled to Benin and Ghana after the 1998 election violence — over 24,500 to Benin and 15,500 to Ghana. Amnesty International's 1999 Togo report documents extrajudicial killings, bodies found in the sea reportedly dropped from aircraft, and systematic torture. The curated figure of 40,000-80,000 is slightly wide at the upper end (UNHCR cites 40,000+ confirmed) but the core event is TRUE.

title: Lomé Peace Agreement on Sierra Leone Signed in Togolese Capital
reason: The Lomé Peace Agreement between the Sierra Leone government and the RUF was signed on July 7, 1999, in Lomé, Togo. The University of Notre Dame Peace Accords Matrix, UN Peacemaker, and Wikipedia all confirm the date, the parties (Kabbah and Sankoh), and Lomé as the signing location. Togo's role as neutral host is accurate.

title: Constitutional Amendment Enables Eyadéma's Lifetime Rule
reason: In December 2002, the RPT-controlled National Assembly — after the opposition boycotted October 2002 legislative elections, giving RPT a two-thirds majority — amended the constitution to remove presidential term limits. The amendments also lowered the minimum presidential age to 35 (preparing for Faure's succession) and added residency requirements targeting Gilchrist Olympio in exile. VOA, Africa Center, and ConstitutionNet confirm all key details.

title: Eyadéma Wins Further Term Amid Boycott
reason: Presidential elections in June 2003 were again boycotted by leading opposition parties. Eyadéma's official tally was 57.2%. International observers noted voter register manipulation and media asymmetry. The elections are documented in State Department human rights reports and GlobalSecurity.org. The pattern of managed elections as legitimation devices, as described in the curated event, is consistent with the scholarly record.

title: Eyadéma Dies — Army Installs Son Faure Gnassingbé
reason: Gnassingbé Eyadéma died on February 5, 2005 aboard a plane near Tunis. The army immediately installed his son Faure, bypassing the constitutional succession provision (requiring the National Assembly speaker to serve as interim). The AU's Alpha Oumar Konaré declared it a military coup, and ECOWAS condemned the dynastic transfer. Wikipedia's article on the 2005 Togolese coup d'état and Britannica confirm all key facts. The age of 39 attributed to Faure is slightly off — he was born 1966, making him 38 in February 2005.

title: ECOWAS Pressure Forces Temporary Reversal — Then Faure Wins Election
reason: Under ECOWAS sanctions pressure, Faure stepped down on February 25, 2005 in favour of Bonfoh Abbass. He then ran and officially won the April 24, 2005 election with 60.9%. The post-election death toll is contested: the Togolese League of Human Rights cited 790 killed (not 400-500 as stated), and ECOWAS actually assessed the vote as largely fair while the EU criticised it. The core narrative of ECOWAS pressure, temporary reversal, and violent aftermath is TRUE; the curated death-toll figure (400-500) is an undercount.

title: Ouagadougou Political Accord Signed
reason: The Accord Politique Global (APG) was negotiated in Ouagadougou under Burkina Faso President Blaise Compaoré's facilitation between August 7-19, 2006, with EU and ECOWAS as observers. It provided for a national unity government, revised CENI composition, and a path to legislative elections. The PA-X Peace Agreements database and IRIN News confirm all key details. The accord's partial implementation and EU aid normalisation are accurately described.

title: Legislative Elections Held — RPT Retains Majority
reason: Parliamentary elections on October 14, 2007 saw RPT win 50 of 81 seats. ECOWAS with 152 observers assessed the elections as 'free, fair, and open'; the AU also gave a positive assessment; EU observers noted 'satisfactory conditions.' Critics noted the electoral system allowed RPT to win 62% of seats with 39% of votes. Wikipedia's article on the 2007 Togolese parliamentary election and EU EEAS mission reports confirm all key facts.

title: EU Aid Resumes After 14-Year Suspension
reason: EU development cooperation with Togo was re-established in 2007 (not 2008), after a 14-year hiatus following Article 96 consultations opened in April 2004. EU documentation explicitly states cooperation resumed in 2007. The 14-year suspension (1993-2007) and the Article 96 Cotonou mechanism are confirmed, but the year stated in the curated event is wrong by one year.

title: Faure Gnassingbé Re-Elected in Contested Vote
reason: Faure won the March 4, 2010 presidential election with an official 60.88% against Jean-Pierre Fabre's 33.93%. International observers deemed the election largely free and fair with some procedural problems. ReliefWeb and Wikipedia's article on the 2010 Togolese presidential election confirm the result. The opposition alleged ballot fraud and organised protests. The curated description is accurate.

title: Mass Opposition Protests Demand Constitutional Reform
reason: Beginning in June 2012, an opposition coalition (Collectif Sauvons le Togo / arc-en-ciel alliance) organised mass protests in Lomé demanding restoration of the 1992 constitution's two-term limit. Thousands attended demonstrations in June and August 2012. Wikipedia's article on the 2012-2013 Togolese protests and ConstitutionNet confirm the scale, timing, and demands. The description of these as the largest protests since the early 1990s is consistent with the record.

title: Legislative Elections — RPT-Successor UNIR Wins Majority
reason: Parliamentary elections on July 25, 2013 gave UNIR (founded April 2012 to replace RPT) a commanding majority of 62 of 91 seats. The ANC won 16. No large-scale fraud was reported during voting. Wikipedia's article on the 2013 Togolese parliamentary election and Docslib academic analysis confirm all key facts. The curated event correctly identifies UNIR as the RPT successor renamed in 2012.

title: Phosphate Production Decline and Economic Diversification Push
reason: Togo did experience declining phosphate production challenges through the 2010s and accelerated port and logistics investment. The Lomé Container Terminal's third dock entered service in October 2014 and became a regional hub for landlocked Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. The Business Year and TiL Group confirm the port's growing regional significance. The characterisation of Togo diversifying toward port/logistics and agro-processing is accurate, though 2014 is the specific year the port expansion became operational rather than the diversification push being announced.

title: Faure Gnassingbé Wins Third Presidential Term
reason: Faure won the April 25, 2015 presidential election with 58.75% against Jean-Pierre Fabre's 34.95%. The Constitutional Court validated the result on May 3, 2015. International and national observers declared the election generally free and fair. The curated figure of 58.8% is accurate. France 24 and Wikipedia's article on the 2015 Togolese presidential election confirm all key details.

title: Massive Anti-Government Protests Demand Term Limits and Democratic Reform
reason: From August 19, 2017, PNP leader Tikpi Atchadam launched protests that grew into a coalition of 14 opposition parties (C-14) demanding restoration of the 1992 constitution and two-term limits. Protests occurred across the country including Sokodé, Bafilo, and Lomé. Internet shutdowns and security force violence were documented. Wikipedia's article on the 2017-2018 Togolese protests and Africa's A Country reporting confirm the scale and demands. The description is accurate.

title: Security Force Violence During Protests — Dozens Killed
reason: Togolese security forces fired live ammunition during the August-September 2017 protests. Amnesty International documented individual killings including Rachad Maman shot in Bafilo on September 20, 2017. Death tolls ranged from the government's admission of 2 in Sokodé to opposition claims of 7+, with security sector impunity confirmed by Amnesty and HRW. The Tem community in central Togo was specifically targeted. The curated claim of 'at least a dozen' deaths across the protest wave is plausible given documented individual cases.

title: Constitutional Amendment Offers Prospective Term Limits — Not Retroactive
reason: Following ECOWAS-mediated inter-Togolese dialogue, the National Assembly passed a constitutional amendment in 2019 (not May 2018) reinstating a two-term presidential limit but applying it prospectively — meaning Faure's existing terms would not count. The Africa Center, ConstitutionNet, and ISS Africa confirm the non-retroactive design that effectively allows Faure to govern until at least 2030. The year in the curated event (2018) is off by one — the vote was in May 2019 — but the event description is otherwise accurate.

title: Internet Shutdowns Used to Suppress Protest Coordination
reason: The Togolese government shut down mobile internet access from September 5-11, 2017 (and on subsequent occasions in 2017-2018) during protests. OONI data, Access Now, and the Internet Society Pulse confirm the September 2017 shutdown. An ECOWAS court later ruled the internet shutdown violated human rights law. The year stated (2018) refers to the broader 2017-2018 protest period during which shutdowns occurred; the phenomenon began in 2017.

title: Legislative Elections — UNIR Retains Supermajority
reason: The legislative elections described occurred on December 20, 2018, not 2019. UNIR won 59 of 91 seats. The main C-14 opposition coalition boycotted. IPU Parline and Wikipedia's article on the 2018 Togolese parliamentary election confirm the December 2018 date. The year attributed in the curated event is wrong by one year, making this a material factual error.

title: Faure Gnassingbé Elected to Fourth Presidential Term
reason: Faure won the February 22, 2020 presidential election with an official 72% against Agbéyomé Kodjo's 18.4%. Kodjo alleged fraud; he was subsequently arrested. Al Jazeera, Africanews, and France 24 confirm the result, the 72% official figure, and the fraud allegations. The election occurred during COVID-19's emergence though international observer presence was not notably reduced at that time.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic — Government Mobilises Emergency Response
reason: Togo declared a state of health emergency on April 1, 2020, imposed a nationwide curfew, and launched the Novissi digital mobile-money cash transfer programme. World Bank published detailed results (April 2021) citing 572,852 beneficiaries between April-September 2020, 373,858 women among them. The programme's machine-learning targeting of the poorest was publicly praised by the World Bank as a model for Africa. All details confirmed.

title: Jihadist Attacks Begin in Northern Togo
reason: The first attack on Togolese soil occurred on the night of November 9-10, 2021, in Sanloaga village, Kpendjal prefecture (no casualties). A deadlier attack in May 2022 with ~8 soldiers killed was the first JNIM-claimed attack inside Togo. The Long War Journal and Stratfor confirm the November 2021 first incursion and the 2022 JNIM claim. The event description correctly identifies JNIM (Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin) as the group and the Savanes/Burkina Faso border as the locus.

title: State of Emergency Declared in Savanes Region
reason: Togo declared a state of security emergency in the Savanes region in June 2022 (not 2021 as stated) in response to escalating jihadist incursions. Togo First and Africanews confirm the June 2022 date of the declaration. The curated event attributes it to 2021 but the formal state of emergency came in 2022; however the underlying security crisis and civilian displacement began in late 2021. The year is off by approximately one year.

title: Togo Joins Sahel Security Architecture as Coastal States Seek Help
reason: Togo deepened security cooperation with France, the US (AFRICOM), and neighbouring coastal states through the Accra Initiative (Ghana, Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, Togo, Burkina Faso — established 2017, with a multinational joint force announced in November 2022). France's FM visited Togo in 2023 calling it a 'pivotal role' partner. The Hill and Africa Center confirm US-Togo security cooperation and Togo's balancing act as France's influence declined after Sahel coups.

title: Lomé Port Expansion Cements Regional Logistics Role
reason: The Lomé Container Terminal reached 35 gross moves per hour in Q2 2022. With a 16.6-meter depth accommodating post-Panamax vessels up to 24,000 TEU, the port serves as the primary maritime gateway for landlocked Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. TiL Group, UNISCO, and US Embassy Togo all confirm the port's deepwater status and landlocked country service. The event correctly places the cement of Togo's logistics hub status in 2022.

title: Allegations of Wagner Group Contacts Surface
reason: No specific reporting confirms Togolese military officials held preliminary contacts with Wagner Group in late 2022 or 2023. Wagner's known footprint was concentrated in Mali, Burkina Faso, CAR, and Sudan; searches found no credible sourced report of Togo-Wagner contacts. The government denial is consistent with a complete lack of documentary evidence. The curated event may conflate Togo's geographic proximity to Wagner-active Burkina Faso with direct contacts that cannot be verified.

title: Savanes Insurgency Intensifies — Dozens of Soldiers Killed
reason: In 2023, Togo recorded 14 attacks killing 66 people total (ACLED). A February 2023 attack on Tola and Gningou villages killed 31 civilians — the deadliest single jihadist attack in Togo to date. President Faure acknowledged approximately 40 security force deaths since the insurgency's start. Africanews ('Togo: Over 30 dead in terrorist attacks in 2023'), Soufan Center, and ACLED data confirm the intensification. The description of 'dozens of soldiers killed' is broadly consistent with official and independent counts.

title: Togolese Phosphate Exports Reach Highest Level in Decade
reason: Togo First confirms a 'significant surge in phosphate output and sales' in the post-Ukraine period; SNPT produced 1,517,478 metric tons of rock phosphate in 2023. However, no source found explicitly confirms this as the highest export level in more than ten years. The Ukraine-war fertiliser price windfall did benefit phosphate exporters, but whether Togo specifically reached a decade-high remains unverified within the available search results.

title: New Constitution Shifts Togo to Parliamentary System
reason: On March 25, 2024, the National Assembly adopted a new constitution shifting Togo from a presidential to a parliamentary system, abolishing direct presidential elections and creating the position of 'President of the Council of Ministers' elected by parliament for six-year terms without term limits. No referendum was held despite constitutional requirements. Africanews, Al Jazeera, and the Library of Congress confirm the March 25 date, the constitutional content, and the absence of a referendum.

title: Faure Becomes 'President of Council of Ministers' Under New System
reason: Following the April 29, 2024 legislative elections in which UNIR won 108 of 113 seats, Faure Gnassingbé was designated President of the Council of Ministers — the new chief executive role under the parliamentary constitution. He was formally sworn in on May 3, 2025. Xinhua, France 24, and Togo First confirm the sequence. The event's description of the role combining executive primacy with indefinite tenure without direct election is accurate.

title: ECOWAS and African Union Criticise Constitutional Process
reason: ECOWAS issued a communiqué on April 15, 2024 criticising the constitutional reforms and announced a fact-finding mission, but its overall response was described by observers as weak and ultimately the bloc (along with the AU and OIF) commended the April 29 elections as peaceful. The AU's response was not a strong condemnation. The curated event overstates the force of regional criticism — ECOWAS did criticise but then effectively endorsed the outcome. The EU reportedly reviewed its partnership framework, but evidence of a formal EU suspension is not confirmed.

title: Opposition Suppressed Ahead of April Legislative Elections
reason: Ahead of the April 29, 2024 elections, opposition leaders reported arrests, campaign harassment, a French journalist was arrested and expelled, and the Catholic Church's observer request was rejected. Major opposition parties boycotted or were marginalised; UNIR won 108 of 113 seats. BISI, Freedom House, and the Africa Center confirm the systematic constraints on opposition participation and the near-total sweep by the ruling party.

title: Savanes Emergency Extended — Humanitarian Displacement Grows
reason: The state of emergency in Savanes was extended multiple times in 2024, with parliament extending it again in August 2024 to facilitate military operations. ReliefWeb and GIEWS October 2024 brief confirm 423,165 people in Togo experiencing crisis-level acute food insecurity, Savanes worst-affected, with 32,000 IDPs registered by UNHCR. The curated figure of 350,000 displaced/food-insecure is somewhat below confirmed reports of 423,165 food-insecure, but the humanitarian crisis is real and accurately described.

title: British Togoland Votes to Join Ghana, Not Togo
reason: A UN-supervised plebiscite on May 9, 1956 resulted in 58% of voters in British Togoland choosing integration with the Gold Coast (Ghana) — though the vote split geographically, with the north strongly for and south against. The UN General Assembly ratified the outcome in December 1956. British Togoland integrated with Ghana on March 6, 1957. Wikipedia's article on British Togoland and the 1956 plebiscite confirm all key facts. The curated event's note on the Ewe partition and the 1967 political divide is accurate.

title: Lomé III Convention Renews ACP-EC Development Partnership
reason: Lomé III was signed on December 8, 1984 at Lomé, Togo, between the EEC and 71 ACP states; it came into force for trade in March 1985 and for aid provisions in May 1986. EU Publications Office and IMF Finance and Development (1985) confirm the date and the Lomé hosting. The curated event's year (1985) refers to the year the convention entered into force, which is a defensible framing, and the characterisation of European realpolitik over conditionality during the Cold War is accurate.

title: High Commission for Human Rights and Reconciliation Established
reason: The 1991 National Conference established transitional institutions including the Haut Conseil de la République (HCR), but a specific 'High Commission for Human Rights and Reconciliation' as described is not confirmed in multiple sources. HRW's 2001 report on government human rights commissions in Africa and OHCHR materials refer to a later 2009 CVJR. A transitional human rights body may have existed but its specific name, mandate, and outcome as described cannot be independently verified from available search results.

title: Diaspora Remittances Become Major Economic Lifeline
reason: By 2005, Togolese diaspora remittances totalled approximately $143 million USD, representing 8.5% of GDP, and CADTM data confirms remittances were 3-6 times higher than bilateral budget aid for multiple years. Diaspora communities are concentrated in France, Germany, Belgium, and West African neighbouring states. The characterisation of remittances exceeding ODA and reflecting political emigration is accurate.

title: Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission Created
reason: The CVJR (Commission Vérité, Justice et Réconciliation) was established by presidential decree in 2005 and became operational on February 25, 2009. It investigated violations from 1958 to 2005, collected 22,415 statements, held 523 hearings, and published its report volumes from 2012. The African Transitional Justice Hub (CSVR) and JusticeInfo.net confirm all key details. Implementation of the 68 recommendations has been slow and underfunded, as stated.

title: West Africa's Largest Solar Plant Opens Near Lomé
reason: The largest solar plant in West Africa opened in Blitta (approximately 267 km north of Lomé, not near Lomé) in June 2021, not 2016. It was a 50 MW facility built by AMEA Power, financed by the West African Development Bank and Abu Dhabi Fund for Development — not the European Investment Bank as stated. The curated event is wrong on the year (2016 vs 2021), location ('near Lomé' vs Blitta), and financing source (EIB vs West African/Abu Dhabi funds).

title: Togo Elected to UN Security Council Non-Permanent Seat
reason: Togo was elected to the UN Security Council as a non-permanent member for the 2012-2013 term (elected in October 2011), not for 2020-2021 as stated, and not in 2019. The UN Security Council membership records and the UN Press release (October 2011) confirm Togo's Security Council term was 2012-2013. The 2019 UNSC election did not include Togo. The event's year (2019) and the claimed 2020-2021 term are both incorrect.
